content: Chinese martial arts, often referred to as Kung Fu and Wushu, are terms that have become synonymous with the martial traditions of China. However, the terms Kung Fu (pinyin: gōngfū) and Wushu (武术) carry distinct meanings. Kung Fu colloquially refers to any skill or accomplishment achieved through hard work and practice, not necessarily related to martial arts. In contrast, Wushu is a more precise term that directly refers to martial activities. Additionally, Wushu has evolved into a modern sport resembling gymnastics, where practitioners perform adapted Chinese martial arts forms (taolu 套路) judged on contemporary aesthetic criteria. The origins of Chinese martial arts trace back to ancient China, where they were developed for self-defense, hunting, and military training. Hand-to-hand combat and weapons practice were integral to the training of Chinese soldiers. Over time, these practices incorporated various philosophies and ideas, expanding their purpose from self-defense to health and self-cultivation. Martial arts ideals have influenced Chinese poetry, fiction, and film, becoming a vital element of Chinese culture. According to legend, the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), who ascended the throne in 2698 BCE, introduced the earliest forms of martial arts to China. He was described as a general who wrote treatises on medicine, astrology, and martial arts. He is also credited with developing the practice of jiao di or horn-butting, which was used in warfare. This evolved during the Zhou Dynasty into a combat wrestling system called jueli or jiaoli (角力), which included techniques such as strikes, throws, joint manipulation, and pressure point attacks. By the Qin Dynasty (221–207 BCE), jiaoli became a sport and is now known as shuai jiao in its modern form. Sophisticated martial arts theories based on the concepts of yin and yang, as well as the integration of hard and soft techniques, were recorded during the Spring and Autumn Period (722–481 BCE). In the Tang Dynasty, sword dances were immortalized in the poetry of Li Bai. During the Song and Yuan dynasties, xiangpu (an early form of sumo) contests were sponsored by the imperial courts. The modern concepts of Wushu were fully developed during the Ming and Qing dynasties. Chinese martial arts are also deeply intertwined with Chinese philosophy. Daoist texts like the Zhuangzi (庄子) and the Tao Te Ching contain principles applicable to martial arts. Confucian texts, such as the Zhou Li (周礼), included archery and charioteering as part of the six arts of the Zhou Dynasty. Sun Tzu's The Art of War (孙子兵法), written in the 6th century BCE, while focused on military strategy, also influenced martial arts principles. Over time, the ideas associated with Chinese martial arts evolved alongside Chinese society, acquiring a philosophical foundation. Daoist practitioners have been engaging in physical exercises like Tao Yin, which resemble Qigong and are considered precursors to Tai Chi Chuan, as early as 500 BCE. In 39–92 CE, the Six Chapters of Hand Fighting were included in the Han Shu (History of the Former Han Dynasty), and Hua Tuo, a renowned physician, created the Five Animals Play (tiger, deer, monkey, bear, and bird) around 220 BCE. These practices reflect the influence of Daoist philosophy on health and exercise, which likely shaped Chinese martial arts to some extent. The Shaolin style of martial arts is one of the most famous traditions. The earliest evidence of Shaolin monks participating in combat is a stele from 728 CE, which documents their defense of the Shaolin Monastery from bandits around 610 CE and their role in the defeat of Wang Shichong at the Battle of Hulao in 621 CE. Between the 8th and 15th centuries, there is no extant documentation of Shaolin combat participation. However, from the 16th to 17th centuries, numerous sources confirm that Shaolin monks practiced martial arts, which had become an integral part of monastic life. These sources include epitaphs, martial arts manuals, military encyclopedias, historical writings, travelogues, fiction, and poetry. The Shaolin monks became renowned for their expertise in armed combat, particularly with the staff (gun 棍), which General Qi Jiguang included in his book Treatise of Effective Discipline. The fighting styles practiced today have evolved over centuries, incorporating forms that emerged later. Examples include Bagua, Drunken Boxing, Eagle Claw, Five Animals, Xing Yi, Hung Gar, Lau Gar, Monkey, Praying Mantis, Fujian White Crane, Wing Chun, and Tai Chi Chuan. The modern perception of Chinese martial arts has been significantly influenced by events during the Republican Period (1912–1949). During this time, martial arts became more accessible to the general public, as many martial artists were encouraged to openly teach their art. Martial arts were also seen as a means to promote national pride and build a strong nation. Training manuals were published, a training academy was established, national examinations were organized, demonstration teams traveled overseas, and numerous martial arts associations were formed. The Central Guoshu Academy (Zhongyang Guoshuguan 中央国术馆), established in 1928, and the Jing Wu Athletic Association (精武体育会), founded by Huo Yuanjia in 1910, are examples of organizations that promoted systematic training in Chinese martial arts. A series of provincial and national competitions were organized by the Republican government starting in 1932 to promote martial arts. In 1936, at the 11th Olympic Games in Berlin, Chinese martial artists demonstrated their art to an international audience for the first time. These events contributed to the popular view of martial arts as a sport. Chinese martial arts began to spread internationally after the end of the Chinese Civil War and the founding of the People's Republic of China (PRC) on October 1, 1949. Many well-known martial artists fled PRC rule and migrated to Taiwan, Hong Kong, and other parts of the world, where they began teaching within overseas Chinese communities and eventually expanded their teachings to include people from other cultures. Within China, the practice of traditional martial arts was discouraged during the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976). Like many aspects of traditional Chinese life, martial arts were subjected to radical transformation to align with Maoist revolutionary doctrine. The PRC promoted the committee-regulated sport of Wushu as a replacement for independent martial arts schools. This new competition sport was disassociated from the self-defense aspects and family lineages of traditional martial arts, which were seen as potentially subversive. In 1958, the government established the All-China Wushu Association to regulate martial arts training. The Chinese State Commission for Physical Culture and Sports created standardized forms for most major arts. During this period, a national Wushu system with standard forms, teaching curricula, and instructor grading was established. Wushu was introduced at both the high school and university levels. The suppression of traditional teaching was relaxed during the Era of Reconstruction (1976–1989), as Communist ideology became more accommodating to alternative viewpoints. In 1979, the State Commission for Physical Culture and Sports created a special task force to reevaluate the teaching and practice of Wushu. In 1986, the Chinese National Research Institute of Wushu was established as the central authority for Wushu research and administration in the PRC. Changing government policies and attitudes toward sports led to the closure of the State Sports Commission in 1998, marking a shift toward a more market-driven approach to sports. As a result, both traditional styles and modern Wushu approaches are now being promoted by the Chinese government. China has one of the longest histories of continuously recorded martial arts traditions, with hundreds of styles that are likely the most varied in the world. Over the past two to four thousand years, many distinctive styles have been developed, each with its own techniques and philosophies. Common themes among styles are often classified by families (家 jiā), sects (派 pài), or schools (门 mén). Some styles mimic animal movements, while others draw inspiration from Chinese philosophies, myths, and legends. Certain styles focus on harnessing qi energy, while others emphasize competition and exhibition. Each style offers a unique approach to self-defense, health, and self-cultivation. Chinese martial arts can be categorized into external (外家拳) and internal (内家拳) styles, as well as by geographic origin, such as northern (北拳) and southern (南拳) styles. Northern styles emphasize fast and powerful kicks, high jumps, and fluid movements, while southern styles focus on strong arm and hand techniques, stable stances, and quick footwork. Examples of northern styles include Changquan and Xingyiquan, while southern styles include Nanquan and Wing Chun. Martial arts can also be classified by religion, imitative styles (象形拳), and more. Training in Chinese martial arts consists of basics, forms, applications, and weapons. Basics (基本功) are essential for progression, as strong and flexible muscles, proper body mechanics, and the management of qi are necessary for performing movements correctly. Basics training includes stretching, stance work, conditioning, meditation, and basic techniques. Internal training focuses on the heart, mind, spirit, breathing, and strength. Stances (步法) are structural postures that form the foundation of a fighter's base. They vary by style and are differentiated by foot position, weight distribution, and body alignment. Stance training can be static or dynamic. Examples include the horse-riding stance (骑马步) and the bow stance. Meditation is an important component of basic training in many systems, used to develop focus, mental clarity, and as a basis for qigong training. Forms (套路) are predetermined sequences of movements practiced as a linear set. They were originally intended to preserve the lineage of a style and were often taught to advanced students. Forms contain literal, representative, and exercise-oriented techniques that are extracted, tested, and trained through sparring. Many believe forms should be practical, usable, and applicable while promoting flow, meditation, flexibility, balance, and coordination. There are two general types of forms: solo forms and sparring forms. Sparring forms are choreographed fighting sets performed by two or more people and are useful for teaching combat concepts. Forms using weapons teach students the extension, range, and technique required to manage a weapon. Today, forms are considered one of the most important practices in Chinese martial arts, though traditionally, they played a smaller role compared to sparring, drilling, and conditioning. Modern forms, particularly in Wushu, have grown in complexity and often include acrobatic movements for visual appeal. This has led to criticism from traditionalists who believe the original value of martial arts is being lost. Some traditionalists argue that forms work is less relevant than sparring and application. Application training involves putting martial techniques into practice. Techniques are based on efficiency and effectiveness, and their teaching varies by style. Sparring simulates combat situations with rules to reduce injury. The subject of application training is controversial, with debates between neo-traditionalists and sport-oriented practitioners. Neo-traditionalists believe martial arts should be proven in actual combat and governed by moral philosophy, while sport-oriented practitioners emphasize sparring to test techniques. Weapons training (器械) is an integral part of most Chinese styles, focusing on conditioning, coordination, and strategy. Weapons are considered extensions of the body, and training progresses from forms to partner work and applications. Most systems include methods for the Eighteen Arms of Wushu (十八般兵器) and specialized instruments specific to the system. Traditional Chinese martial arts often incorporate ethics, known as Wude (武德), which translates to martial morality. Wude encompasses morality of deed (social relations) and morality of mind (inner harmony). The ultimate goal is achieving balance and harmony between wisdom and emotions. The concept of qi (气), or life force, is central to almost all styles. Internal styles cultivate qi differently than external styles. Qi can be strengthened through qigong, which is often integrated into martial arts practice. Some styles focus on directing qi to specific points during attacks, such as in Dim Mak techniques, which resemble acupressure. Advanced qigong practice is sometimes believed to enable physical effects without physical contact, though this is rarely seen outside of movies. Notable practitioners throughout history include Yue Fei, a Song Dynasty general associated with styles like Eagle Claw and Xing Yi, and Ng Mui, a legendary female founder of styles like Wing Chun and Fujian White Crane.
